questions.sharedContext:
1 ‘Anchored’ common subsequences
Recall the definition of longest common subsequence (LCS) from the lecture: the LCS of strings $s_1$ , $s_2$ is
the longest string $s$ such that $s$ is a subsequence of both $s_1$ and $s_2$ , i.e., we can get $s$ by starting at some
point in $s_i$ , reading through, perhaps skipping some letters, and then stopping at some point.

Suppose now our alphabet contains a special ‘anchor’ character * which binds ‘more strongly’ than
ordinary letters: concretely, a string $s$ is an anchored common subsequence if no * is skipped when reading
through the relevant substring of each $s_i$ (note: *s can occur outside the substring of $s_i$ where $s$ occurs).

For example, suppose that $s_1 = A ∗ BCD∗$ and $s_2 = B ∗ CAD$. We would not be allowed to take the
subsequence BC (because this requires skipping a * in $s_2$ ), but we would be allowed to take the subsequence
*CD, which is the longest anchored common subsequence and has length 3.


2 Examples
$s_1 = A ∗ BF ∗ CB$ $s_1 = BFA ∗ B$
$s_2 = F ∗ CAB ∗ D$ $s_2 = CB ∗ A ∗ BB$
LACS = F ∗ CB LACS = A ∗ B $s_1 = ACCBDFBA ∗ BA$
 $s_2 = CBAAF ∗ BAA$
$s_1 = A ∗ B ∗ CD∗$ $s_1 = ∗AC∗$ LACS = CBF ∗ BA or CBA ∗ BA
$s_2 = B ∗ CAD$ $s_2 = ∗BD∗$
LACS = B ∗ CD LACS = ∗∗
questions.text:
1. Provide a dynamic programming algorithm (in pseudocode) to find a longest anchored common
subsequence of two strings. Justify the correctness and analyze the running time of your algorithm.
questions.modelAnswer:
Let $s_1$ and $s_2$ have lengths $n$ and $m$. Define $DP[i][j]$ to be the length of a longest anchored common subsequence of the prefixes $s_1[1..i]$ and $s_2[1..j]$.

The key change from ordinary LCS is that an anchor cannot be skipped once it is inside the considered substring. Therefore, if exactly one of the current last characters is `*`, we are not allowed to drop that `*`; the only possible anchored common subsequence of these prefixes must end before that anchor.

```text
LACS(s1, s2):
    n = length(s1)
    m = length(s2)
    create array DP[0..n][0..m]

    for i = 0 to n:
        DP[i][0] = 0
    for j = 0 to m:
        DP[0][j] = 0

    for i = 1 to n:
        for j = 1 to m:
            if s1[i] == s2[j]:
                DP[i][j] = DP[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
            else if s1[i] == '*':
                DP[i][j] = DP[i - 1][j]
            else if s2[j] == '*':
                DP[i][j] = DP[i][j - 1]
            else:
                DP[i][j] = max(DP[i - 1][j], DP[i][j - 1])

    return DP[n][m]
```

Correctness proof:

We prove by induction on $i+j$ that $DP[i][j]$ equals the length of a longest anchored common subsequence of $s_1[1..i]$ and $s_2[1..j]$.

Base case: If $i=0$ or $j=0$, one prefix is empty, so the longest anchored common subsequence has length $0$. The algorithm sets these entries to $0$.

Inductive step: Assume the claim holds for all smaller prefix pairs.

- If $s_1[i] = s_2[j]$, then an optimal solution may end with this common character. Taking it gives $DP[i-1][j-1] + 1$, and by the induction hypothesis this is optimal for the smaller prefixes plus the matched final character. This is valid for ordinary letters and also for `*`, since matching the two anchors skips neither anchor.
- If $s_1[i] = *$ and $s_2[j] \neq *$, then $s_1[i]$ cannot be skipped inside an anchored substring and cannot be matched to $s_2[j]$. Thus any valid solution for these prefixes must lie before this anchor in $s_1$, so the value is $DP[i-1][j]$.
- Symmetrically, if $s_2[j] = *$ and $s_1[i] \neq *$, the value is $DP[i][j-1]$.
- Otherwise $s_1[i] \neq s_2[j]$ and neither character is an anchor. Then an optimal anchored common subsequence either does not use $s_1[i]$ or does not use $s_2[j]$, so the optimal value is $\max(DP[i-1][j], DP[i][j-1])$.

In every case the recurrence considers exactly the valid possibilities for an optimal anchored common subsequence. Therefore, by induction, $DP[n][m]$ is the length of a longest anchored common subsequence of $s_1$ and $s_2$.

Running time: The table has $(n+1)(m+1)$ entries and each entry is computed in $O(1)$ time, so the running time is $O(nm)$. The space usage is $O(nm)$, or $O(m)$ if only the previous row is stored when only the length is required.

questions.text:
2. Implement your algorithm. The input file will have two lines, each consisting of a string over
alphabet A,B,...,Z,* of length at most 2,000 characters. Your program should output a single
integer n, the length of the longest anchored common subsequence.
Name your program Anchored.java and submit it to Codegrade for testing.
